question: advisor said my stats class from my last school only counts as an elective not for my major. i dont get it, its the same class. can i ask for someone to look at it again

body.answer:
Sorry to hear that!

Yes. If academic approval for a non-general education course equivalency has not yet been established, it may count as elective credit but not toward a particular degree program. You may contact the Convener of the appropriate program to review the course and its potential for transfer credit. If approved, the Convener sends the equivalency approval to the Office of Admissions, which designates someone to update the appropriate systems. [2]

Contact the Center for Student Success (Academic Advising) for guidance on next steps. [20]

- **Admissions**: Phone: (201) 684-7300. Email: admissions@ramapo.edu. Location: McBride House. [33]
- **Center for Student Success (Academic Advising)**: Phone: (201) 684-7441. Email: success@ramapo.edu. Office: D-207. [33]

Sources: [2](https://catalog.ramapo.edu/quicklinks/academicpolicies#transferring-academic-credit1) [20](https://www.ramapo.edu/studentsuccess/faq/) [33](https://www.ramapo.edu/campus-directory/)

question: what laptop should i get for school, mac or windows?

body.answer:
**General answer** (from general knowledge, not Ramapo's pages): Neither is universally better. Choose a Mac if you value battery life, a polished build, and already use Apple devices; choose Windows for more price options, gaming, or software that specifically requires Windows. Check your course’s required apps and budget first, then compare models with at least 16 GB of RAM and enough storage for your work.

Ramapo says business students should get a Windows computer because many applications are only available for Windows. Students in the Susan and Nick Vallario School of Arts, Humanities, and Education may want to consider a MacBook, as many applications for that program are Mac-based. For other students, either Windows or Mac is sufficient. [1]

For sciences, math, computer science, animation, video editing, and other computer-intensive fields, consider a laptop that meets or exceeds the “High-end” recommendations. Ramapo does not recommend Chromebooks because they may not support the same applications as Windows and Mac laptops. [1]

For a Mac, the recommended model is a 13” MacBook Air or 14″ MacBook Pro, with MacOS 15 Sequoia, MacOS 26 Tahoe, or MacOS 27 Golden Gate; M3/M4 or higher CPU; 16 GB or more RAM; and 512GB SSD. High-end: 14” MacBook Pro, M5/M5 Pro or higher, 16 GB or more RAM, and 1TB SSD. [2]

See Ramapo’s [student laptop recommendations](https://www.ramapo.edu/its/student-laptop-recommendations/) for Windows specifications and suggested laptop manufacturers. [1]

**School of Arts, Humanities, and Education Office**: Phone: (201) 684-7365. Email: AHEOffice@ramapo.edu. Office: B-224. [33]

Sources: [1](https://www.ramapo.edu/its/student-laptop-recommendations/) [2](https://www.ramapo.edu/its/student-laptop-recommendations/) [33](https://www.ramapo.edu/campus-directory/)

answer:
**General answer** (from general knowledge, not Ramapo's pages): Neither is universally better. Choose a Mac if you value battery life, a polished build, and already use Apple devices; choose Windows for more price options, gaming, or software that specifically requires Windows. Check your course’s required apps and budget first, then compare models with at least 16 GB of RAM and enough storage for your work.

Ramapo says business students should get a Windows computer because many applications are only available for Windows. Students in the Susan and Nick Vallario School of Arts, Humanities, and Education may want to consider a MacBook, as many applications for that program are Mac-based. For other students, either Windows or Mac is sufficient. [1]

For sciences, math, computer science, animation, video editing, and other computer-intensive fields, consider a laptop that meets or exceeds the “High-end” recommendations. Ramapo does not recommend Chromebooks because they may not support the same applications as Windows and Mac laptops. [1]

For a Mac, the recommended model is a 13” MacBook Air or 14″ MacBook Pro, with MacOS 15 Sequoia, MacOS 26 Tahoe, or MacOS 27 Golden Gate; M3/M4 or higher CPU; 16 GB or more RAM; and 512GB SSD. High-end: 14” MacBook Pro, M5/M5 Pro or higher, 16 GB or more RAM, and 1TB SSD. [2]

See Ramapo’s [student laptop recommendations](https://www.ramapo.edu/its/student-laptop-recommendations/) for Windows specifications and suggested laptop manufacturers. [1]

**School of Arts, Humanities, and Education Office**: Phone: (201) 684-7365. Email: AHEOffice@ramapo.edu. Office: B-224. [33]

Sources: [1](https://www.ramapo.edu/its/student-laptop-recommendations/) [2](https://www.ramapo.edu/its/student-laptop-recommendations/) [33](https://www.ramapo.edu/campus-directory/)

question: should i get an ipad or a laptop for college

body.answer:
**General answer** (from general knowledge, not Ramapo's pages): A laptop is the safer choice if you can only get one: it handles essays, spreadsheets, coding, and exam or course software more reliably. An iPad is great for handwritten notes, reading, and drawing, but may be limiting as your only device. If you already have access to a computer, an iPad can be a useful add-on.

Ramapo’s recommendation depends on your program: business students should invest in a Windows computer; students in the Susan and Nick Vallario School of Arts, Humanities, and Education may want to consider an Apple computer such as a MacBook; for other students, either a Windows or Mac laptop is sufficient. Students in sciences, math, computer science, animation, video editing, and other computer-intensive fields should consider a computer meeting or exceeding the “High-end” recommendations. Ramapo does not recommend Chromebooks. [1]

The recommendation is for a laptop, not an iPad. Ramapo’s page doesn’t say whether an iPad is sufficient for college, so I don’t have verified information about that. See Ramapo’s laptop recommendations: [https://www.ramapo.edu/its/student-laptop-recommendations/](https://www.ramapo.edu/its/student-laptop-recommendations/) [1]

**School of Arts, Humanities, and Education Office**: Phone: (201) 684-7365. Email: AHEOffice@ramapo.edu. Office: B-224. [30]

answer:
**General answer** (from general knowledge, not Ramapo's pages): A laptop is the safer choice if you can only get one: it handles essays, spreadsheets, coding, and exam or course software more reliably. An iPad is great for handwritten notes, reading, and drawing, but may be limiting as your only device. If you already have access to a computer, an iPad can be a useful add-on.

Ramapo’s recommendation depends on your program: business students should invest in a Windows computer; students in the Susan and Nick Vallario School of Arts, Humanities, and Education may want to consider an Apple computer such as a MacBook; for other students, either a Windows or Mac laptop is sufficient. Students in sciences, math, computer science, animation, video editing, and other computer-intensive fields should consider a computer meeting or exceeding the “High-end” recommendations. Ramapo does not recommend Chromebooks. [1]

The recommendation is for a laptop, not an iPad. Ramapo’s page doesn’t say whether an iPad is sufficient for college, so I don’t have verified information about that. See Ramapo’s laptop recommendations: [https://www.ramapo.edu/its/student-laptop-recommendations/](https://www.ramapo.edu/its/student-laptop-recommendations/) [1]

**School of Arts, Humanities, and Education Office**: Phone: (201) 684-7365. Email: AHEOffice@ramapo.edu. Office: B-224. [30]

Sources: [1](https://www.ramapo.edu/its/student-laptop-recommendations/) [30](https://www.ramapo.edu/campus-directory/)

question: is it better to buy textbooks or rent them

body.answer:
**General answer** (from general knowledge, not Ramapo's pages): Renting is usually cheaper if you only need the book for one class and don’t plan to keep it. Buying makes more sense if you’ll reuse it, need to write in it, or can resell it later. Compare the total rental cost and return deadlines with the used-book price and resale value.

Ramapo says you can buy or rent textbooks; some are also available as eBooks for certain classes. It does not say which option is better. [1]

To find your required books, log into web self-service, click “Student Services and Financial Aid,” select Registration, then select “Buy Books Now from efollett.com.” This generates the required textbook list based on your current course registration. You may choose to rent or buy books new or used, and pick them up at the bookstore or have them shipped to your home. [4]

The Bookstore says renting textbooks can save up to 80% off the price of a new book. [15]

**Financial Aid**: Phone: (201) 684-7549. Email: finaid@ramapo.edu. Office: E-210. [32]

Sources: [1](https://www.ramapo.edu/orientation/families/faq/) [4](https://www.ramapo.edu/orientation/faq-2/) [15](https://www.ramapo.edu/bookstore/) [32](https://www.ramapo.edu/campus-directory/)

A course reserve is an item that a professor has asked to be set aside for their students, because it has been assigned as part of their course. These items can be owned by the library, but they can also be borrowed from the professor themselves. These items are in high demand, which is why they have been put aside and given different policies. What kind of course reserve items are there? Library Owned Course Reserve Books These are library books that the professor has assigned in a course; they are normally available at the library but can be put on course reserve for up to one year. Library Owned Course Reserve DVDs These are library DVDs that the professor has assigned in a course; they are normally available at the library but can be put on course reserve for up to one year. Professor Owned Course Reserve Books These are books or other materials that a professor owns personally and has chosen to bring in and lend them to the library to allow their students access to them. These are especially valuable as they do not belong to the library and are only available through the generosity of the professors. Professor Owned Course Reserve DVDs These are DVDs that a professor owns personally and has chosen to bring in and lend them to the library to allow their students access to them. These are especially valuable as they do not belong to the library and are only available through the generosity of the professors. Photocopy Reserves These are articles are portions of books that have been photocopied and printed out to be checked out for students usage, if they are not available online. E-Reserves E-reserves can be short articles, book-portions, case studies, etc. that have been scanned and uploaded to the library’s online catalog at the request of professors. These items can only be viewed by an @ramapo.edu email, but they can be accessed on any device with internet access. For more information on How can I check out a course reserve? To check out a course reserve, please bring the item’s call number (which can be found in our online catalog) to the circulation desk. Tell the call number to the student aide at the desk and they will retrieve the item from the storage area and check it out to you. How long can I check out a course reserve for? All course reserve items can only be checked out for 4 hours at a time, and they have strictly imposed late fees. Please plan accordingly. Can I take a course reserve outside of the library? All library owned course reserves can be removed from the library, but a few specific professor-owned items can only be used within the library due to their importance. These items will be clearly marked with a note in our online catalog as well as a clearly printed label on the front of the items themselves. How can I find a course reserve item on the library website? **General answer** (from general knowledge, not Ramapo's pages): Renting is usually cheaper if you only need the book for one class and don’t plan to keep it. Buying makes more sense if you’ll reuse it, need to write in it, or can resell it later. Compare the total rental cost and return deadlines with the used-book price and resale value.

Ramapo says you can buy or rent textbooks; some are also available as eBooks for certain classes. It does not say which option is better. [1]

To find your required books, log into web self-service, click “Student Services and Financial Aid,” select Registration, then select “Buy Books Now from efollett.com.” This generates the required textbook list based on your current course registration. You may choose to rent or buy books new or used, and pick them up at the bookstore or have them shipped to your home. [4]

The Bookstore says renting textbooks can save up to 80% off the price of a new book. [15]

**Financial Aid**: Phone: (201) 684-7549. Email: finaid@ramapo.edu. Office: E-210. [32]

question: how do i get better at public speaking

body.answer: **General answer** (from general knowledge, not Ramapo's pages): Practice out loud in short, regular sessions, and record yourself to spot one thing to improve at a time. Organize each talk around a clear main point with a simple opening and ending. Slow down, pause between ideas, and look at a few friendly faces rather than trying to memorize every word. Start with low-pressure audiences and build up gradually.

Handshake helps you explore career interests and find internships with alumni, companies, and organizations: [http://ramapo.joinhandshake.com/](http://ramapo.joinhandshake.com/) [2] The Career Center can assist with your job search and provide resources through Handshake and other job sources. [3]

**Cahill Career Development Center**: Phone: Main Office (201) 684-7444; ASB Office (201) 684-7675. Email: careercenter@ramapo.edu. Main Office: C-209; ASB Office: ASB-513. [24]

Sources: [1](https://www.ramapo.edu/careercenter/four-year-plan/) [2](https://www.ramapo.edu/careercenter/presidents-internship-list/) [3](https://www.ramapo.edu/careercenter/get-started/) [24](https://www.ramapo.edu/campus-directory/)

question: i need my flu shot record for my clinical, where do i get it

body.answer:
The pages don’t say specifically how to get a flu shot record for clinical. Health Services handles immunization and health paperwork; contact them to ask. Their immunization information page is [https://www.ramapo.edu/health/immunization-info/](https://www.ramapo.edu/health/immunization-info/) [13].

**Health Services**: Phone: (201) 684-7536. Location: Near the campus South Gate entrance at the corner of Route 202 and Hornbeam Road. [33]

Sources: [13](https://www.ramapo.edu/adult-students/contacts/) [33](https://www.ramapo.edu/campus-directory/)

question: whats a good laptop for graphic design classes

body.answer:
**General answer** (from general knowledge, not Ramapo's pages): For graphic design classes, look for a laptop with at least 16 GB of RAM, a modern Core i5/Ryzen 5 or better processor, and a color-accurate screen (ideally close to full sRGB coverage). A 512 GB SSD is a useful minimum; choose 1 TB if you’ll store lots of large files. A dedicated graphics card helps with 3D or video work, but isn’t essential for most 2D design. Check your course software’s requirements before buying.

Ramapo says students in certain majors, including animation, video editing and other computer-intensive fields, should consider a computer that meets or exceeds the “High-end” column. For other students, either Windows or Mac is sufficient. It does not specifically identify graphic design classes in the quoted guidance, so I can’t verify which category applies to you. Chromebooks are not recommended because they often do not support the same applications as Windows and Mac laptops. [2]

The listed high-end specifications are Windows 11; Intel Core Ultra X7/X9 or AMD Ryzen AI 9 (HX-class); 32 GB or more RAM; 1TB SSD; and 1920 x 1080 or better screen resolution. For video/animation students, discrete graphics with at least 2GB GPU, 4GB GPU recommended. [3]

Ramapo links to Apple, Dell, HP and Lenovo student/education vendor pages, and says discounts may change and education pricing is not always the lowest; research options before purchasing. [5]

For questions about a purchase, contact the IT Help Desk at helpdesk@ramapo.edu. [2]

- **Purchasing Department**: Phone: (201) 684-7496. Email: purchase@ramapo.edu. Office: D-118. [14]
- **IT Help Desk**: Phone: (201) 684-7777. Email: helpdesk@ramapo.edu. Location: 4th floor of the Learning Commons. [14]

Sources: [2](https://www.ramapo.edu/its/student-laptop-recommendations/) [3](https://www.ramapo.edu/its/student-laptop-recommendations/) [5](https://www.ramapo.edu/its/student-laptop-recommendations/) [14](https://www.ramapo.edu/campus-directory/)

answer:
**General answer** (from general knowledge, not Ramapo's pages): For graphic design classes, look for a laptop with at least 16 GB of RAM, a modern Core i5/Ryzen 5 or better processor, and a color-accurate screen (ideally close to full sRGB coverage). A 512 GB SSD is a useful minimum; choose 1 TB if you’ll store lots of large files. A dedicated graphics card helps with 3D or video work, but isn’t essential for most 2D design. Check your course software’s requirements before buying.

Ramapo says students in certain majors, including animation, video editing and other computer-intensive fields, should consider a computer that meets or exceeds the “High-end” column. For other students, either Windows or Mac is sufficient. It does not specifically identify graphic design classes in the quoted guidance, so I can’t verify which category applies to you. Chromebooks are not recommended because they often do not support the same applications as Windows and Mac laptops. [2]

The listed high-end specifications are Windows 11; Intel Core Ultra X7/X9 or AMD Ryzen AI 9 (HX-class); 32 GB or more RAM; 1TB SSD; and 1920 x 1080 or better screen resolution. For video/animation students, discrete graphics with at least 2GB GPU, 4GB GPU recommended. [3]

Ramapo links to Apple, Dell, HP and Lenovo student/education vendor pages, and says discounts may change and education pricing is not always the lowest; research options before purchasing. [5]

For questions about a purchase, contact the IT Help Desk at helpdesk@ramapo.edu. [2]

- **Purchasing Department**: Phone: (201) 684-7496. Email: purchase@ramapo.edu. Office: D-118. [14]
- **IT Help Desk**: Phone: (201) 684-7777. Email: helpdesk@ramapo.edu. Location: 4th floor of the Learning Commons. [14]

Sources: [2](https://www.ramapo.edu/its/student-laptop-recommendations/) [3](https://www.ramapo.edu/its/student-laptop-recommendations/) [5](https://www.ramapo.edu/its/student-laptop-recommendations/) [14](https://www.ramapo.edu/campus-directory/)
